alignment.note: καί / ܘ (prefixed to ܥܢܐ) / Et — coordinating conjunction.

Greek uses the finite aorist ἀπεκρίθη ('answered'); the Vulgate renders it with the present participle respondens, a periphrastic Semitic-style construction common in the Gospels; the Peshitta's ܘܥܢܐ is finite, matching the Greek but absorbing the conjunction. Syriac index 0 is shared with the conjunction group above by morphological necessity.

The Greek dative αὐτῷ ('to him', i.e. to Jesus) is present in NA28 but has no counterpart in either the Vulgate or the Peshitta, both of which leave the indirect object implicit; this is a frequent minor Western/Syriac economy with redundant pronouns.
ἐκ τοῦ ὄχλου / ܡܢ ܟܢܫܐ / de turba — partitive prepositional phrase; Greek and Vulgate carry the article, Syriac uses the emphatic state.
εἶπεν / ܘܐܡܪ / dixit (with following colon) — verb of speaking introducing direct discourse.
ἤνεγκα / ܐܝܬܝܬ / attuli — first-person aorist/perfect, 'I brought'.
τὸν υἱόν μου / ܒܪܝ / filium meum — 'my son'; Syriac compresses the possessive into the suffixed ܒܪܝ, where Greek and Latin use separate pronouns.
πρὸς σέ / ܠܘܬܟ / ad te — 'to you'; Syriac again suffixes the pronoun to the preposition.

Greek uses an attributive participle phrase ἔχοντα πνεῦμα ἄλαλον ('having a mute spirit'), and the Vulgate mirrors it with habentem spiritum mutum; the Peshitta restructures with the existential relative ܕܐܝܬ ܠܗ ('who has [lit. there-is to-him] a spirit') and renders 'mute' analytically as ܕܠܐ ܡܡܠܠܐ ('that does not speak'), a typical Syriac periphrasis for the single adjective ἄλαλος.
